Obituary: Rich Rowland (1964-2026)

September 6, 2026 ~ Sam Gazdziak
i
Rate This

Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 13:30
Instaread

RIP to Rich Rowland, who spent parts of 6 seasons during the 1990s as a big-league catcher. He died on August 27 at the age of 62. Rowland played for the Detroit Tigers (1990-1993) and Boston Red Sox (1994-1995).

Richard Garnet Rowland was born in Cloverdale, CA, on February 25, 1964. His road to professional sports had a few detours along the way. He was an all-star basketball player at Cloverdale High School and an excellent catcher as well, but he was best known for football. He set the school’s record for passing yards in 1981 as the quarterback and won the Most Valuable Player Award in the North Central League I Conference. Rowland graduated in 1982 and went to Ventura College, but he only lasted there a year. He went to work in the timber industry, keeping a toe in athletics by joining the Cloverdale Merchants, a local baseball team. The Merchants coach, Dan Stacy, sent word to Mendocino College baseball coach Lefty Olguin about the team’s hard-hitting catcher. Olguin convinced Rowland to temporarily put aside his job as a heavy equipment operator, which paid $25,000 a year, to play baseball. With the blessing of his wife Carol, he agreed to give baseball another shot. He joined the Mendocino College Eagles in 1988 and batted .500 with 6 home runs, and he became the best defensive catcher in the Bay Valley Conference. He was drafted by the Detroit Tigers in the 17th Round of the 1988 June Amateur Draft, completing his trek from high school athlete to lumberjack to professional ballplayer. “I feel real fortunate,” Rowland said. “It wouldn’t have happened without Lefty. It was always a dream.”

Rowland joined the Tigers’ Rookie-Level Appalachian League team in Bristol, TN, in 1988. The 24-year-old was among the older players in the league (not that anybody knew that), and he batted .274 in 56 games. He hit just 4 home runs as he adjusted to pro ball, but his development impressed his coaches. “He went through a period where he wasn’t throwing the ball as well as he could, and recently he had a little trouble with high, inside fastballs,” said manager Rich Magnante. “But he made the necessary adjustments and is really playing well again.” Rowland made up for lost time with a rapid rise through the minors after that debut season. He moved up to Class-A Fayetteville of the Sally League in 1989 and hit .272 with 9 homers in 108 games. He batted .272 again in 1990 while splitting the season between Double-A London and Triple-A Toledo, but he raised his home run total to 15. He was rewarded for his good season with a promotion to Detroit in September.

Rowland made his major-league debut as the designated hitter for the Tigers on September 7, 1990, against Milwaukee. Detroit outfielder Milt Cuyler made his debut in the same game. Rowland went 0-for-2 and drew a walk against Brewers starter Teddy Higuera. He went behind the plate on September 9, and he got his first major-league hit, a double, off Milwaukee’s Narciso Elvira. He made periodic starts as a catcher or DH for the final month of the season and appeared in a total of 7 games, with 3 hits in 19 at-bats. Rowland was considered the team’s top catching prospect, but the Tigers acquired slugging catcher Mickey Tettleton in a trade with Baltimore in January 1991. Suddenly, Rowland’s path to the majors was blocked. While Tettleton homered 31 times as Detroit’s primary catcher, Rowland batted .272 in the minors for the third straight season, with 13 homers and 68 RBIs. Detroit brought Rowland to the majors in September, but he made it into only 4 games and had a hit in 4 at-bats. Detroit’s catching needs were covered by Tettleton and Chad Krueter in 1992, and the team let it be known that it would entertain offers for Rowland. “He’s got [expansion teams] Miami and Denver and about four other teams who might be interested in him,” said Detroit manager Sparky Anderson. “If he has a good year, he’ll be a valuable piece of merchandise.” Rowland set career highs with 25 home runs and 82 RBIs for Toledo in 1992, though his batting average dropped to .235. He played in 6 games for Detroit in September and had 3 hits in 14 at-bats for a .214 batting average.

Detroit came to see that Tettleton wasn’t an ideal fielding catcher, and he was subsequently moved all around the field as well as DH in 1993. However, Krueter came into his own and took over the role of starting catcher. Anderson wanted an additional reliever on the active roster rather than a third catcher, and so Rowland was returned to Toledo for another year. “If anyone has a right to complain, it’s Rowland,” Anderson said later that season. “He deserves to be in the big leagues and he knows it. But all he has done is keep his mouth shut and gone out and played.” Rowland wasn’t exactly mute about the subject of his career. “Number one, I’d like to be in the big leagues in Detroit, but I’m not getting any younger and catchers’ life expectancy in the big leagues is not good,” he said during spring training. “I’m not saying that I’ve hit my peak, but I know I’m ready to produce, and I’ll do it with any big league team.” Rowland was promoted to the majors in August, giving him the first taste of baseball outside of September. He played occasionally and spent much of August and September batting over .300. At one point, he had doubles in 3 straight starts, but those starts occurred over a period of two weeks. Rowland played 21 games with Detroit, more than he had in the previous three seasons combined. A 1-for-3 game with an RBI single off Milwaukee’s Higuera on September 21 left him with a .294 batting average. However, Rowland went hitless over his next 4 games, and that 0-for-12 dry spell greatly affected his end-of-season stats. He had 10 hits for a .217/.294/.283 slash line, with 4 RBIs and 5 walks.

Spring training began for Detroit in early 1994, and it didn’t look like the upcoming season would be any different for Rowland. “I have been in the Tigers’ camp six years and every year I go away disappointed,” he told The Blade (Toledo, OH), in March. “I’m in my prime right now. Actually, I’ve been in my prime. I’ve wasted the last couple years.” Rowland may have been more accurate than anyone knew. He had just turned 30 years old, but there’s a decent chance that nobody in the Detroit organization knew it. Rowland’s baseball cards show him being born in 1967, and that article in The Blade specifically said he was 27 years old. Had Rowland taken the traditional high school-to-college-to pro ball route, he would have been about 27. But his job as a lumberjack had added years to that timeline. In baseball’s earlier days, it was pretty common for ballplayers to knock a few years off their age to improve their odds of reaching the majors. And you would think that in the 1990s, teams would be a little more scientific in their scouting. On the other hand, the internet was a fledgling concept, so a scout couldn’t just Google a player’s information. It didn’t become common knowledge that Rowland was three years older than anyone realized until after he departed the Tigers, when the Boston Globe discovered that he had graduated from high school in 1982, not 1985.

Ultimately, Rowland’s opportunity would not come with Detroit. Blade columnist John Gugger noted that the Tigers didn’t like the catcher’s defense and thought he was too stiff behind the plate. Rowland had a .984 fielding percentage with the Tigers, and he didn’t commit any passed balls. However, he threw out just 4 of 21 baserunners for a 19% success rate, far below league average. It’s a small sample size based on limited playing time, but the Tigers must have felt it was enough. On April 1, the team traded Rowland to the Boston Red Sox for catcher John Flaherty. The Sox had a gaping hole behind the plate. Starter Tony Pena had departed the team as a free agent, so the catching duties in 1994 were split between Damon Berryhill, Dave Valle and Rowland. Rowland spent the entire year in the majors, and he played in a career-high 46 games. He made his first start of the year on April 18 against Chicago and drove in a run with a single off Wilson Alvarez. The White Sox won the game 12-1, thanks to 3 home runs by Tim Raines. On May 8, he connected off Yankees pitcher Terry Mulholland for his first career home run, in his 46th big-league game. Given the opportunity to play at least semi-regularly, Rowland clubbed 9 home runs to lead all Red Sox catchers — Berryhill and Valle had 7 between them. Three of them came in a 5-game stretch from June 4 to June 8. He saved his best power display for his final game of the year. On August 10, Rowland launched a solo homer off Minnesota’s Jim Deshaies in the second inning, and then he added a 2-run blast off reliever Mike Trombley in the sixth. Those two home runs were the second and third of the series against the Twins, and after struggling through the month of July, Rowland was hitting over .400 through August. But the very next day, the players went on strike, and the remainder of the season was ultimately canceled. Rowland slashed .229/.295/.483 with 3 doubles and 9 home runs. He drove in 20 runs and drew 11 walks against 35 strikeouts. Defensively, he may have had a .972 fielding percentage, but he raised his caught-stealing rate to 36.4% (12 out of 33 baserunners), which was above league average.

Rowland finally acknowledged the age discrepancy when approached by the Globe in April 1995, after the strike had been settled. “It made a difference getting signed,” he said, “but I really don’t want to make a big deal of it. I’d forgotten about it. So it really didn’t enter my mind until this last year. I didn’t talk about it last year, and really, I’m not going to talk about it this year. Because I feel I can play as a 28-year-old. So what difference does it make how old you are if you do the job?” Rowland had been acquired by Boston to be a long-term solution behind the plate, but when his true age became common knowledge, the team decided he was no longer the catcher of the future. Two of the moves that Boston made before the season began were to sign free agent catchers Mike Macfarlane and Bill Haselman. Macfarlane was about a month younger than Rowland, and Haselman was 29 years old. Rowland began the season as the team’s third catcher, but his chances to play were few. He made rare starts and entered other games as a late-inning replacement, but he got into just 14 games through mid-June, with 5 hits in 29 at-bats. He was designated for assignment on June 20, 1995, ending his major-league career. He joined Boston’s Triple-A team in Pawtucket and batted .258 in 34 games. Rowland became a free agent after the season and spent 1996 with Syracuse, Toronto’s Triple-A team. He hit .226 with 8 homers, and then he appeared briefly in the minors for San Francisco in 1997 before retiring from the game.

Rowland played in parts of 6 seasons in the major leagues and appeared in 98 games. He slashed .213/.281/.365, with 8 doubles and 9 home runs among his 49 hits. He drove in 26 runs and scored 22 times. He had a career .646 OPS and 68 OPS+. He also had a .977 fielding percentage as a catcher and threw out 17 of 58 baserunners. Rowland also played 7 innings at first base and 4 innings at third base, handling a total of 8 chances without an error. He was a career .254 hitter with 105 home runs in 9 minor-league seasons as well.

Rowland was honored by Cloverdale High School in 1995 and donated one of his Red Sox jerseys to be displayed in the school. He and his family settled in Cloverdale, and he returned to a career in the timber industry. In addition to his wife Carol, he is survived by two sons, Richie and Robby. Both boys became baseball players themselves, with their father coaching them. Richie spent a season in the Arizona Diamondbacks system, and Robby had an extensive pitching career in the minors, independent ball and foreign leagues. Robby Rowland has become a popular baseball social media figure with nearly 250,000 followers on Instagram (@robbyrow12). He has posted some wonderful family photos since his father’s death. Also, Robby is looking for video of Rich Rowland’s 9 major-league home runs from 1995. On the outside chance that anyone reading this is connected with MLB Media, it would be appreciated if you could get in touch with Robby and help fulfill this request.
